notes.meaning: Nahash, the king of the Ammonites, marched up and surrounded the town of Jabesh-gilead to attack it. The terrified townspeople offered to make a treaty and serve him if he would spare them. They felt completely alone and did not expect their fellow Israelites across the Jordan River to come help.

Nahash agreed only on the cruel condition that he gouge out the right eye of every man, bringing shame on the whole nation. In battle, an ancient soldier held a shield that covered his left eye, so losing his right eye left him unable to fight. Nahash wanted to humiliate Israel and make sure these men could never rebel against him.

The leaders of Jabesh asked for a seven-day pause so they could send messengers across Israel to see if anyone would come to save them. Nahash boastfully granted the request because he was confident no one would dare oppose him. The town promised to surrender to his harsh terms if no rescuer arrived in time.

The messengers arrived at Saul's hometown of Gibeah and told the people what Nahash had said. The people of Gibeah burst into loud weeping because their tribe shared close family ties with Jabesh-gilead. Even though they felt deep sorrow, they had no plan of their own to fix the crisis.

Saul was just coming home from the fields behind his plowing oxen when he heard the crying. Even though he had been chosen as king, he had humbly returned to everyday farm work until God gave him a clear call to act. He cared about his neighbors and asked why everyone was in tears.

As soon as Saul heard the report, the Holy Spirit rushed upon him with great power, and he burned with deep anger. This was not a selfish tantrum, but a righteous anger against the cruel threat facing God's people. God gave Saul the boldness and strength he needed to step up and lead.

Saul butchered two oxen, cut them into pieces, and sent the meat across the land with a stern warning. Anyone who refused to march behind Saul and Samuel would have their own cattle treated the same way. God placed a deep reverence and fear in the hearts of the people, and they answered the call as one united body.

Saul counted his troops at Bezek, gathering 300,000 men from Israel and 30,000 from the tribe of Judah. Bezek was located near the river crossing, placing the army in an ideal spot to march straight to Jabesh-gilead. The massive turnout showed how quickly the nation rallied behind their new leader.

Saul told the messengers to assure Jabesh-gilead that rescue would arrive by noon the very next day. When the messengers brought this promise back to the town, the people rejoiced with great relief. Knowing that help was really coming turned their fear into hope.

The men of Jabesh told Nahash that they would surrender the next day and let him do whatever pleased him. They deliberately hid the news of Saul's approaching army so the Ammonites would let their guard down. This clever trick made the enemy feel completely safe just before the rescue arrived.

Saul split his army into three divisions and attacked the Ammonite camp just before sunrise. They caught the enemy completely by surprise and fought them until the hottest part of the day. The Ammonites were scattered so badly that no two soldiers were left together.

Thrilled by the great victory, the soldiers turned to Samuel and demanded the deaths of the men who had earlier opposed Saul's rule. They wanted to punish the rebels who had doubted that Saul could ever save them. Their victory made them eager to wipe out any remaining opposition.

Saul stepped in and declared that no one would be executed on a day when the Lord had rescued Israel. Instead of getting even with his critics, Saul gave all the credit and praise to God. He showed true mercy and wisdom by choosing peace over revenge.

Samuel invited all the people to travel to Gilgal to renew Saul's kingship. Gilgal was an important place of worship where Israel had first camped after crossing into the promised land. Samuel used this time of national unity to confirm Saul's authority in front of everyone.

The entire nation gathered at Gilgal and officially confirmed Saul as king in the presence of the Lord. They sacrificed peace offerings, which were special thanksgiving meals shared with God and the community, and celebrated with great joy. The whole country was united and thankful for what the Lord had done.
